subChunks.title: The Reproducibility Crisis in Science
subChunks.hookHtml:
'In 2011, Bayer HealthCare published a study,' Theodora said. 'They had attempted to reproduce the key findings from published academic studies before deciding whether to invest in drug development. Their conclusion: they could reproduce only 25% of the results. In 2012, Amgen published a similar analysis: they could reproduce only 11 of 53 landmark oncology papers — 21%. The papers they could not reproduce had been cited hundreds of times, had attracted millions in follow-on funding, and had shaped clinical trial strategies. And most of them were wrong.'

'The phrase "reproducibility crisis" was coined in the early 2010s, but the phenomenon it named was not new. What was new was the data: systematic, large-scale, multi-laboratory attempts to replicate published findings that produced devastating results. Psychology's Open Science Collaboration attempted to replicate 100 psychology experiments from top journals in 2015. Only 36–47% replicated. Social psychology fared worst. Priming effects — participants primed with words related to aging walking more slowly — largely evaporated. Ego depletion, the idea that willpower is a limited resource, has not survived replication. Power posing's cortisol effects did not replicate.'

'The crisis is not equally distributed. Physics and chemistry have relatively high replication rates. Clinical medicine and some areas of psychology and neuroscience have low replication rates. The pattern implicates specific methodological and incentive features, not science as a whole.'
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What Reproducibility Means

Reproducibility terminology is contested but the most useful distinctions are: computational reproducibility — given the same data and code, can you reproduce the same results? (mostly about data and code sharing); analytical reproducibility — given the same data, does a different analyst reach the same conclusions? (often not, as shown by the Many Analysts study); replicability — running a new study with the same methods on a different sample, does it produce the same result?; generalisability — does the effect found in one population/context generalise to others?

These are distinct failures: a study can be computationally reproducible but not replicable (all original analyses can be reproduced but the effect does not appear in a new sample); or replicable in some populations but not generalisable (a social psychology effect in US undergraduates may not generalise cross-culturally).

Causes of the Crisis

Publication bias: positive results are published; null results are suppressed. Ioannidis (2005) proved mathematically that in a research field with many tested hypotheses, high false positive rates, and publication bias, most published findings will be false positives. The probability that a published positive result reflects a true effect decreases as: the effect size decreases, the study power decreases, the number of tested hypotheses increases, and publication bias strengthens. Under realistic field conditions, the majority of published findings in some areas are estimated to be false positives.

Questionable Research Practices (QRPs): p-hacking, HARKing, selective outcome reporting, and flexible stopping rules. John et al. (2012) surveyed psychologists: 63% admitted to selectively reporting studies that 'worked'; 58% admitted to continuing data collection until significant results were achieved. These are not exceptional behaviours — they are typical responses to incentive structures that reward significant results.

Underpowered studies: Most published studies in psychology and neuroscience are substantially underpowered, increasing false positive rates and guaranteeing that the reported effect sizes of significant results are inflated (winner's curse). Button et al. (2013) found median statistical power in neuroscience studies was 8–31% — meaning that most true effects in the field would not be detected by the typical study.

Experimenter degrees of freedom: Simmons, Nelson, and Simonsohn (2011) demonstrated through simulation that any two-condition study with multiple measured outcomes, covariate flexibility, and data-peeking can achieve p < 0.05 ~61% of the time with a true effect size of zero. The 'garden of forking paths' (Gelman) — all the legitimate-seeming analytic choices a researcher can make — inflates false positive rates far beyond the nominal α.

Small sample sizes in high-variance fields: Social psychology and neuroimaging studies often involve tens of participants measuring highly variable responses. Small samples produce noisy estimates that fluctuate dramatically across studies — making replication failures likely even for true effects.

The Open Science Response

The response to the reproducibility crisis has been substantial and partially effective. Pre-registration: specifying hypotheses, sample size, and analysis plan before data collection. Distinguishes confirmatory from exploratory analyses. Journals (including those requiring registered reports) show substantially lower rates of significant results in pre-registered studies, consistent with QRP-reduction. Open data and code: Sharing de-identified data and analysis code enables computational reproducibility checking and facilitates meta-analysis. FAIR principles guide data sharing. OSF (Open Science Framework) is the major platform. Large-scale replication projects: the Open Science Collaboration, Many Labs projects, Psychological Science Accelerator — multi-laboratory, pre-registered, well-powered replication attempts providing the most reliable estimates of effect sizes and generalisability. Reproducibility-incentivising publishing formats: registered reports, results-blind review. Statistical reform: moving from significance testing to estimation (effect sizes + confidence intervals), Bayesian approaches, equivalence testing. Some journals now discourage or ban p-values.

The Crisis Beyond Psychology

Biomedical research: Prinz et al. (Bayer, 2011), Begley and Ellis (Amgen, 2012). The FDA Amendments Act 2007 required clinical trial registration — reducing outcome switching in registered trials. Preclinical animal research: Sena et al. (2010) showed that >50% of published stroke model drug effects do not translate to clinical benefit, partly attributable to publication bias and selective reporting in preclinical literature. Nutrition science: epidemiological associations between food and health outcomes are notoriously difficult to replicate across cohort studies, driven by confounding, measurement error in dietary recall, and researcher degrees of freedom in defining exposures. Genomics: the GWAS era has been mostly more reliable than candidate gene studies — pre-specified hypotheses, large samples, strict significance thresholds — but early candidate gene studies (the 'candidate gene problem') replicated poorly.

storyBeats.text: 'Ioannidis's 2005 paper — "Why Most Published Research Findings Are False" — is the most-cited paper in PLoS Medicine and probably in the top fifty most-cited papers in any journal. It used simulation, not new data. It proved mathematically that under realistic assumptions about prior probability of hypotheses, effect sizes, and publication bias, the majority of published findings in many fields will be false positives. It was attacked. It was verified repeatedly. It was correct.'

'Button et al.'s median power in neuroscience of 8–31%: that means most studies could not detect a true effect even if it existed. A study with 20% power will fail to replicate 80% of the time even when the effect is real. When power is low and publication selects for significant results, the published effects are necessarily inflated — the winner's curse operating in full force.'

'The garden of forking paths is not about dishonesty. Most researchers making QRP choices are not consciously deceiving anyone. They are making legitimate-seeming decisions — should I exclude this outlier? should I control for this covariate? should I include this mediator? — that, collectively and without pre-specification, inflate false positive rates dramatically. The system is not producing bad scientists. It is producing a bad system that turns normal scientific behaviour into systematic error.'

'Registered reports in my view are the single most important methodological reform since randomisation. If you commit to the hypothesis and analysis plan before seeing the data, the forking paths collapse to a single pre-specified path. The published result is what you found, not what you found after looking. The evidence base becomes a more honest map of reality.'

'The crisis is not uniformly distributed. Physics has built-in reproducibility checks — results that conflict with established theory are immediately challenged, and the theory-experiment feedback loop is tight. Chemistry has quantitative predictions and precise measurement. Genomics improved dramatically with GWAS discipline. The fields in crisis share features: small samples, high-variance outcomes, many analytic degrees of freedom, and an incentive structure that rewards significant novel findings above all.'

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what the reproducibility crisis is and why even honest, well-meaning scientists can produce research results that turn out to be wrong.
learningObjectives: Distinguish computational reproducibility, analytical reproducibility, replicability, and generalisability as distinct failure modes
Explain Ioannidis's mathematical argument for why most published findings may be false positives and identify the field conditions that increase this probability
Evaluate the effectiveness of pre-registration, open data, and registered reports as responses to the reproducibility crisis
Analyse why the crisis is worse in some fields than others, identifying the methodological and incentive features that distinguish high- and low-replication-rate areas
commonMistakes: Treating the reproducibility crisis as evidence that science is untrustworthy — it is evidence that the publication system selects for positive results, not that the underlying scientific method is flawed

Conflating a failure to replicate with proof that the original finding was fraudulent — underpowered studies can fail to replicate true effects; the winner's curse means replications find smaller effects even when the effect is real
Assuming pre-registration alone resolves the crisis — pre-registration prevents p-hacking but does not address underpowered studies, poor measurement, or analytical errors
Treating all scientific fields as equally affected — the crisis is concentrated in fields with specific methodological and incentive features; physics and chemistry are substantially less affected
assessmentCriteria: Correctly explains the Ioannidis argument, identifying the specific parameters that drive the false positive probability (prior, power, publication bias)
Accurately describes at least three specific QRPs and explains the mechanism by which each inflates false positive rates
Evaluates open science reforms critically — identifying their benefits and their limitations for different types of research
Analyses a specific discipline's replication landscape, connecting its replication rate to identifiable methodological and incentive features
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Evaluating a Replication Failure

The 'ego depletion' hypothesis (Baumeister 1998) proposed that willpower is a limited resource: exerting self-control on one task reduces capacity for subsequent self-control tasks. The original study found that participants who resisted eating cookies subsequently gave up faster on an unsolvable puzzle. The study was published in JPSP (n = 67). Multiple replications followed over 15 years, mostly confirming the effect. In 2016, a pre-registered 23-lab replication (n = 2,141) found a near-zero effect (d = 0.04, 95% CI: -0.07 to 0.15). Proponents argued the replication failed because it used different protocols; critics argued this exemplified the original studies' fragility.

  1. Explain why the original n = 67 study was almost certainly underpowered for detecting the reported effect size, and what consequence this has for the published effect estimate.
  2. The 23-lab study was pre-registered. Why does pre-registration strengthen the evidential value of the near-zero result?
  3. Proponents of ego depletion argue that the replication used 'different protocols'. Evaluate this argument: when is a methodological difference a legitimate reason to discount a replication failure?
  4. What should happen to the 200+ papers that built on the ego depletion finding? What are the researchers' ethical obligations?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Underpowered original study: The original study (n = 67, roughly 33 per condition) could reliably detect only large effects (d ≥ 0.5 at 80% power with α = 0.05). If the true effect is smaller (as subsequent meta-analyses and the large replication suggest), the original study would have been well under 50% powered. The consequence: when an underpowered study does produce a significant result, the winner's curse applies — the published effect size is necessarily inflated above the true effect size, because only the largest observed values cross the significance threshold. Thus, even if ego depletion is a real (small) effect, the published d ≈ 0.6 is a biased overestimate. Downstream studies powering on this inflated estimate would be underpowered for the true effect.

2. Pre-registration value for null results: An un-pre-registered null result is ambiguous: the researcher could have run the study, found d ≈ 0, and then decided not to publish (publication bias). Pre-registration creates a public record before data collection that the study was planned, the hypotheses specified, and the sample size determined. The null result therefore cannot be attributed to selective non-reporting — it must be reported regardless of outcome. This removes the most important alternative explanation for the null finding and substantially increases its evidential weight against the ego depletion hypothesis.

3. 'Different protocols' argument: Methodological differences can legitimately explain replication failures when: (a) the original finding is explicitly modality-specific or context-specific; (b) the difference in protocol is theoretically meaningful (e.g., different manipulation of the independent variable); (c) the original authors specified the boundary conditions in advance. None of these applies cleanly to the ego depletion case: the original theory was general, not protocol-specific; the protocol differences (computer-based vs. paper tasks) were not theoretically motivated in advance; and the replication protocol was designed in consultation with the original authors. When proponents of an effect invoke 'different protocols' only after a replication fails, this is a post-hoc immunisation strategy — a classic protective belt adjustment (Lakatos) that makes the theory unfalsifiable. The argument is not always wrong but requires specific theoretical justification, not post-hoc invocation.

4. Ethical obligations for follow-on researchers: (i) Researchers who built on ego depletion findings should note the failure to replicate in any future publications — not doing so is a form of selective reporting. (ii) Meta-analyses in the field should be updated to include the large replication and correct for publication bias (e.g., using trim-and-fill or Bayesian correction). (iii) Clinical or applied programmes based on ego depletion (e.g., workplace productivity interventions, educational programmes) should be flagged as lacking robust evidence until further replication. (iv) Authors are not ethically required to retract papers reporting the original findings if they were conducted honestly — unlike in cases of fraud — but they should write letters to journals noting the replication context. The scientific community has no fully satisfactory mechanism for updating the evidence base when a finding fails to replicate; registered reports and living systematic reviews are partial solutions.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: The field of social priming — the claim that incidental exposure to a concept (e.g., words associated with aging, money, or achievement) unconsciously influences behaviour — showed dramatic effects in the 2000s but has largely failed to replicate in the 2010s–2020s. Write a 350-word analysis: (a) explain what methodological features of the original priming literature made replication failures predictable in retrospect; (b) evaluate whether the replication failures constitute proof that priming effects do not exist, or merely that the published effect sizes are unreliable; (c) apply the Lakatos framework to the social priming research programme — is it progressive, degenerating, or in transition?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(a) Predictable failures in retrospect: The original priming literature had multiple features that in hindsight predicted replication problems. (i) Small samples (N = 20–80) combined with large claimed effects (d = 0.5–1.0): large effect sizes from small samples are almost always inflated due to the winner's curse. (ii) Single-lab studies with highly specific protocols: John Bargh's famous 'elderly priming walking speed' study was conducted by a single lab with specific confederate-rated dependent measures — highly vulnerable to experimenter expectation effects. (iii) Soft, flexible dependent measures: behaviours like walking speed, paper-and-pencil performance, and donation amounts allow substantial measurement flexibility. (iv) No pre-registration: the published studies represent the successes from many attempts; the failures are in the file drawer. (v) No incentive to replicate within labs: high-impact publication norms favoured novel over replication studies, so internal non-replications were suppressed.

(b) Proof of absence or unreliable effect sizes? The large pre-registered replication failures are strong evidence against the large effects reported in the original literature — d = 0.5+ social priming effects are very likely absent in the original populations studied. However, they do not definitively prove that priming effects of smaller magnitude (d = 0.1–0.2) do not exist. Such effects are: (i) potentially below the detection threshold of adequately powered individual studies; (ii) potentially highly context-dependent, appearing only under specific stimulus conditions. The honest conclusion is that the original effect sizes were dramatically inflated, that large behavioural priming effects are very likely false, and that small effects remain an open empirical question requiring large, pre-registered, multi-laboratory studies with a priori hypotheses about moderating conditions.

(c) Lakatos framework: The social priming research programme had a hard core (unconscious cognition influences behaviour through associative activation) and a protective belt (specific stimulus types, laboratory conditions, dependent measures). In its heyday (2000–2013), it appeared progressive: generating many novel predictions, each confirmed in the original lab. This was, in retrospect, a pseudo-progressive programme — the novelty of predictions was real but their confirmations were artefacts of QRPs rather than genuine effects. Since 2015, the programme has been clearly degenerating: repeated failures to replicate core predictions, absence of novel successful predictions, and increasing reliance on post-hoc boundary condition explanations that immunise the hard core without generating new testable predictions. The programme may not be dead — smaller, context-specific priming effects may exist — but the version that dominated the 2000s literature is a textbook case of a degenerating research programme.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The tendency for published significant effect sizes to overestimate true effects, because underpowered studies produce significant results only when the observed effect is inflated by sampling variability.

Large-scale collaborative replication efforts in which the same study is replicated simultaneously across many laboratories worldwide, providing the best available estimates of effect sizes and moderators.

Gelman and Loken's term for the multiple implicit analytic decisions (inclusion criteria, covariate choice, outlier handling) that, even without conscious p-hacking, inflate false positive rates when not pre-specified.

rabbitHoleTerms.term: Positive predictive value (PPV) of a study
rabbitHoleTerms.description: The probability that a statistically significant result reflects a true effect, which decreases as prior probability of the hypothesis, statistical power, and threshold decrease, and as publication bias increases.

A statistical approach that tests whether an observed effect is small enough to be considered practically zero — addressing the limitation of null hypothesis testing, which can only fail to reject, not positively establish, a null effect.

A free, open-source platform for research documentation, pre-registration, and data sharing maintained by the Center for Open Science — the primary infrastructure for pre-registration in psychology and many other fields.

questions.questionHtml: According to Ioannidis (2005), which combination of conditions most increases the probability that a published finding is a false positive?
options: Low prior probability of the hypothesis being true, low statistical power, and strong publication bias toward positive results
High prior probability of the hypothesis being true, low effect size, and many tested hypotheses
Large sample size, strict significance threshold, and broad hypothesis testing
High statistical power, many researchers in the field, and open data sharing
questions.correctAnswer: Low prior probability of the hypothesis being true, low statistical power, and strong publication bias toward positive results
questions.explanationHtml: Ioannidis's formula for positive predictive value (PPV) of a published finding: PPV = (1−β)π / [(1−β)π + α(1−π)], where π is the prior probability of the hypothesis, β is the false negative rate (1−power), and α is the significance threshold. PPV decreases when π is low (exploratory fields, many unlikely hypotheses tested), when power is low (underpowered studies inflating false positive rates relative to true positives), and when publication bias is high (negative results suppressed, inflating the proportion of positives in the literature). These three conditions together produce the worst-case scenario for literature reliability.

questions.questionHtml: A psychology study (n = 40) reports d = 0.8, p = 0.02. A large pre-registered replication (n = 1,200) finds d = 0.09, 95% CI [-0.02, 0.20]. How should a scientist interpret the original finding after seeing the replication?
options: The large replication provides much stronger evidence; the original effect of d = 0.8 was likely inflated by low power and the winner's curse — the true effect is probably very small or zero
The original study must be fraudulent — a d = 0.8 effect that cannot be replicated indicates data fabrication
The two studies are irreconcilable and the effect is simply unknown — more studies are needed before any conclusion is drawn
The original study should be trusted because it was peer-reviewed; the replication may have used different protocols that explain the discrepancy
questions.correctAnswer: The large replication provides much stronger evidence; the original effect of d = 0.8 was likely inflated by low power and the winner's curse — the true effect is probably very small or zero
questions.explanationHtml: A well-powered replication (n = 1,200 provides >99% power to detect d = 0.3) finding d = 0.09 with CI excluding d = 0.8 strongly suggests the original estimate was inflated. The original n = 40 study was underpowered for anything below d ≈ 0.6; if a true effect of d ≈ 0.09 exists, the original finding reached significance only because sampling variability produced an inflated estimate (winner's curse). This is not fraud — it is the predictable consequence of underpowered studies. The correct response is to update downward: the most reliable estimate of the true effect is from the large pre-registered replication, not the original study.

questions.questionHtml: Pre-registration is proposed as a solution to the reproducibility crisis. Which specific weakness of pre-registration is most important for scientists to understand when evaluating pre-registered studies?
options: Pre-registration prevents p-hacking but does not address underpowered studies, poor measurement validity, or errors in analysis execution — a pre-registered study can still produce a false positive for all these reasons
Pre-registration requires peer review before data collection, which significantly slows the pace of scientific discovery
Pre-registration is only effective for randomised experiments and cannot be applied to observational or longitudinal research designs
Pre-registration eliminates the distinction between confirmatory and exploratory research, making all findings equally uncertain
questions.correctAnswer: Pre-registration prevents p-hacking but does not address underpowered studies, poor measurement validity, or errors in analysis execution — a pre-registered study can still produce a false positive for all these reasons
questions.explanationHtml: Pre-registration addresses one major source of false positives (researcher degrees of freedom — the flexibility to p-hack, HARK, or selectively report). It does not address: (i) insufficient statistical power — a pre-registered underpowered study still inflates false positive rates; (ii) poor measurement validity — if the dependent variable does not measure what the hypothesis requires, the pre-registered analysis is irrelevant; (iii) execution errors — analytical mistakes that are consistently applied; (iv) poor construct operationalisation. Pre-registration is a valuable but partial reform. Its most important function is making the distinction between confirmatory and exploratory analyses visible and honest — it does not guarantee truth.
